items.excerpt: ETH Zurich physicists unveiled PLATON, a particle detector that swaps millions of tiny components for a single block of light-producing material, reading particle tracks in fast 3D via a light-field camera, SPAD photon sensors and AI reconstruction. Simulations suggest it could match or beat today's best detectors while being far easier to scale, with spin-off potential for sharper PET medical scans.

A new AI tool from Queensland University of Technology screened 2.6 million cancer papers published between 1999 and 2024 and flagged more than 250,000 as suspicious, matching writing and data patterns seen in known fraudulent work. The system points at one of the largest research-integrity problems in modern science, showing AI turned on the literature that produced it.

Helmholtz researchers combined machine learning with established physical models to reconstruct Atlantic Ocean circulation from 20 years of Argo profiling-float data, extracting more signal from sparse measurements than physics-only methods. The hybrid approach sharpens understanding of key circulation systems that drive climate.

North Carolina State University researchers built an AI model, BINND, that predicts which DNA molecules will bind to each other with 83.5% accuracy after training on 144 million sequence pairs, beating prior methods by at least 10%. Better modeling of these hypercomplex binding relationships could aid biomedical diagnostics and DNA computing.

Psychologist Michael Hogan describes research using AI-driven analytics to code non-verbal behavior such as silence during group work at millisecond precision, finding that identical pauses carry different meanings by context. The takeaway: the hard problem is not teaching AI to notice behavior, but to interpret it in context.

Quanta surveys a new class of thermodynamic computers that harness random thermal fluctuations as a computational resource rather than fighting them, aiming to run generative-AI algorithms with orders-of-magnitude less energy. Physicists like Normal Computing's Patrick Coles argue exploiting thermodynamics could reshape the hardware substrate of AI.
